Users can select sites and dates, then compare sunlight, shadows, potential solar charging periods, Earth visibility, and communication windows in one mission workspace. The concept addresses the challenge of weighing changing lighting and line-of-sight conditions across multiple locations without relying on difficult-to-interpret reports. Its importance is that it could make those trade-offs easier to understand and explain for mission planners, educators, and the public. The proposed build starts with clearly labeled illustrative data, then adds terrain and NASA SPICE-derived geometry with validated visibility calculations.
details:
PROJECT ORECX is a concept for an interactive lunar mission simulator focused on south-pole landing sites. Users choose candidate locations and mission dates, then play or scrub through time to see how sunlight, shadows, and Earth’s position change. A “Horizon Window” presents the Sun and Earth from the lander’s perspective, making potential solar charging periods and direct communication windows easier to understand. Users can compare sites, explore notional battery impacts, and create a report explaining mission trade-offs.

The project could help mission planners, educators, and the public explore complex conditions through a visual, hands-on experience. Its intended impact is to make site comparisons easier to understand and communicate, while supporting informed decisions. The creative element is combining a lander-level horizon view with a time-based simulator and mission challenge in one workspace.

The proposed prototype uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Three.js for a 3D Moon view, Python for calculations, and Chart.js for timelines. The plan calls for sample sites and clearly labeled illustrative data first, followed by lunar terrain and NASA SPICE data, verified visibility calculations, and validation. The team considered changing illumination, terrain obstruction, time and coordinate handling, battery assumptions, communication visibility, usability, and the need to distinguish geometric visibility from terrain-blocked line of sight.
